title: Your First PHP Program
keywords: executing a php file from the command line
subtopics: Executing a PHP file from the command line.
learning_outcomes: Explain what your first php program contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: creating a php file.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: PHP runs in the PHP runtime and is often used to generate dynamic web responses and command-line output. In a normal web request, the browser receives the response, not the original PHP source. In this lesson, focus on creating a php file; then compare it with writing a simple php statement. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use your first php program when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: PHP runs in the PHP runtime and is often used to generate dynamic web responses and command-line output. In a normal web request, the browser receives the response, not the original PHP source. For your first php program, begin with creating a php file. Also distinguish writing a simple php statement; executing a php file from the command line; displaying output. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Your First PHP Program
content_blocks.code:
<?php
$file = tempnam(sys_get_temp_dir(), "php-course-");
if ($file === false) { throw new RuntimeException("Cannot create temp file"); }
file_put_contents($file, "ready\n");
echo trim((string) file_get_contents($file)) . PHP_EOL;
unlink($file);
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet as example.php. Run `php -l example.php` to check syntax, then run `php example.php` locally when the example has no external-service or framework prerequisites. Some examples are syntax-only illustrations and require the noted extension or framework to run meaningfully.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Use the smallest representative example, make expected behavior explicit, and test normal plus boundary inputs.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for your first php program from top to bottom. Start by identifying creating a php file, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
